B: High-density materials that absorb thermal energy during the day and release it gradually as temperatures drop.
C: The design and orientation of a building to maximize natural light and climate control without mechanical systems.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Passive Solar: C; Thermal Mass: B; Functional Zoning: A

activities.title: Orientation Analysis
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the relationship between site orientation and thermal comfort. Model the placement of a 'North' arrow on a sample floor plan. Explicitly explain: 'In our climate, northern exposure is critical for winter solar gain, while western exposure requires shading to mitigate summer heat load.' Provide a worked example of how to sketch ventilation arrows indicating prevailing South-East breezes across the floor plan, ensuring airflow crosses the living zones.
activities.studentsDo: Analyse the provided site footprint to identify optimal sun paths and ventilation flow. Complete the site orientation plan by marking the North arrow, shading glazing, and zoning spaces based on thermal requirements.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Orient your site plan by drawing the North arrow. 2. Shade the northern glazing areas. 3. Annotate the plan with labels identifying 'Private Zones' (bedrooms/study) and 'Service/Utility Zones' (bathrooms/laundry/kitchen). 4. Draw arrows indicating the path of prevailing South-East cooling breezes.
activities.questioning:
question: What occurs if your primary living area is oriented strictly to the South in the Yeppoon climate?
expected: The living area will remain in shadow during winter, lacking passive solar heat gain. It will require higher energy inputs for heating and may feel damp or uncomfortable.
question: Why is it structurally advantageous to cluster 'Service/Utility Zones' along the western or southern boundary?
expected: These zones act as thermal buffers. They are less sensitive to natural light requirements and can insulate the living zones from the harsh afternoon heat of the western sun.
activities.scaffolding:
Passive Solar Design Guidelines (Yeppoon): 
- North: Maximise glazing for winter sun; use eaves for summer shading. 
- South: Minimise glazing; use for ventilation. 
- East: Early morning sun (good for bedrooms). 
- West: Minimal openings; high thermal mass or shading required to mitigate heat.
activities.eLearning: Use SketchUp orientation tool or a compass app to verify site directionality against local maps: https://www.livingstone.qld.gov.au/
activities.transition: Transition to digital modelling, applying these site constraints to your 3D footprint dimensions.

Model the following: 1. Select the Rectangle tool (R). 2. Click once to originate, move cursor, then type '6000,6000' and Enter. 3. Emphasize that these inputs are standard Australian residential ceiling heights and material thicknesses.

activities.questioning:
question: Why is typing dimensions mathematically superior to dragging the mouse freehand for architectural modelling?
expected: Typing dimensions ensures precise scale and accurate modelling, which is required for real-world construction feasibility and cost estimation.
question: How does using the Offset tool (F) change your approach to creating walls compared to drawing individual lines?
expected: The Offset tool creates a consistent boundary equidistant from the original shape, ensuring uniform wall thickness across the entire footprint.
activities.scaffolding: Reference the SketchUp Shortcut Key Map provided on the whiteboard: R = Rectangle, F = Offset, P = Push/Pull, M = Move, O = Orbit. Precision constraints: Type '6000,6000' for base, '200' for wall thickness, '2400' for wall height.

activities.questioning:
question: What is the primary difference between a Group and a Component regarding editing?
expected: A Group is unique geometry; a Component is an instance-based object. Editing one component instance propagates changes to all copies, whereas groups must be edited individually.
question: Why is 'stickiness' a significant issue when modelling complex architectural forms in SketchUp?
expected: Un-grouped geometry merges faces and edges upon contact, making it nearly impossible to move or isolate specific structural elements without breaking the entire model.
activities.scaffolding: Group: A container that locks geometry together to prevent interaction with adjacent elements. Component: An intelligent object that allows for mass updates across multiple instances, critical for repetitive architectural elements like walls, doors, or windows.

lessons.title: Engineering Sustainable Off-Grid Systems
lessons.learningGoal: Explain the engineering principles behind off-grid energy, water, and waste systems.

orientate.smartStart: Recall three sustainability pillars previously explored in this unit and identify which one is most critical for 'Doomsday' survival scenarios.
orientate.learningGoalDisplay: I can explain the engineering principles behind off-grid energy, water, and waste systems

activities.title: Defining Off-Grid Technologies
activities.teacherDoes: Introduce the concept of 'Resource Autonomy' as the primary design driver for off-grid engineering. Explicitly define key terminology: Photovoltaic (conversion of solar flux to DC electricity), Atmospheric Water Generation (extraction of potable water via condensation cycles), and Closed-loop waste management (conversion of waste biomass into nutrient inputs or energy). Model an example by analysing a standard domestic system and highlighting where resource leakage occurs when systems are not 'closed'.
activities.studentsDo: Complete the 'Off-Grid Systems Definition Matrix' in the workbook. Use the provided technical context to match the terminology to the correct engineering function.
activities.visibleInstructions: Access the workbook provided. Using the terminology list on the left, match each engineering system to its correct functional definition from the bank provided below.
activities.questioning:
question: Why might a reliance on Atmospheric Water Generation be statistically risky in high-temperature, arid climates?
expected: Variable humidity levels directly correlate to water yield; low dew points render the system inefficient compared to catchment methods.
question: What is the critical failure point in a closed-loop waste management system if the decomposition phase is disrupted?
expected: The nutrient cycle ceases, causing waste accumulation and a total loss of input resources for the agricultural or energy components of the system.
activities.scaffolding: 1. Photovoltaic: Semiconductors (e.g., silicon) generate current when exposed to photons. 2. Atmospheric Water Generation (AWG): Utilises cooling coils to drop air temperature below dew point. 3. Closed-loop waste management: A circular system where biological waste is processed via anaerobic digestion or composting to yield resources.
activities.eLearning: Students review technical specifications for local infrastructure to identify if these systems are implemented. Refer to Livingstone Shire Council website for regional waste management policy context.
activities.transition: Transition from definitions to comparative systems analysis, moving into SketchUp modelling to simulate these system placements.

activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the 'Matrix of Suitability' approach. Model how to audit a standard 50m² footprint for an off-grid cabin. Use the example: 'Solar PV has a low mechanical maintenance requirement, making it highly reliable for remote locations, whereas wind turbines, while efficient, have high mechanical wear.' Direct students to use the system audit table to justify their site selection.
activities.studentsDo: Audit the three provided resource systems against the listed criteria in the workbook. Select the most suitable system for a high-wind, coastal environment versus an inland, high-sunlight environment.

activities.questioning:
question: Which system provides the highest reliability if the site is near the coast, considering typical weather patterns in the Capricorn Coast region?
expected: Wind Turbine, due to the consistent coastal sea breezes providing a reliable kinetic energy source.
question: Why is 'Low Maintenance' a critical design factor for off-grid survivalist engineering?
expected: Remoteness limits access to specialist parts and technical support, meaning systems must be durable and easy to service by non-experts.
activities.scaffolding: Reliability: The system's ability to operate continuously despite adverse weather. Footprint: The total physical land area required for infrastructure. Maintenance: The frequency and technical complexity of servicing required to prevent failure.
activities.eLearning: Students review the 'Livingstone Shire Council' sustainability guidelines via the provided website to contextualise environmental constraints.

question: Why is the Component function more efficient than Grouping for repetitive structural elements?

question: What is the consequence of 'exploding' a component within an architectural model?

question: How does the distance between your resource source and the storage zone affect the mechanical complexity of your design?
expected: Increased distance introduces higher friction loss, the need for additional pumping hardware, and increased material requirements.

Economic lens: Initial construction cost versus maintenance over 20 years (long-term viability). Social lens: Impact on accessibility, tourism appeal, and community safety (human wellbeing). Direct students to the workbook, emphasising that effective shelter design requires balancing all three.
activities.studentsDo: Define the three sustainability lenses in the workbook by matching the correct concept to its specific pillar, drawing on the theory provided in the scaffolding bank.
activities.visibleInstructions: Use the definition bank to complete the table by matching each sustainability lens to its correct description.
activities.questioning:
question: Why might a low-cost, high-pollution material fail the economic lens when analysed over a 50-year lifecycle?
expected: Because while the initial capital cost is low, the lifecycle costs—including maintenance, environmental remediation, and potential health-related liabilities—create a greater long-term financial burden.
question: How does the social lens influence our specific 'Doomsday Shelter' design?
expected: It shifts the focus from purely structural integrity to user experience, occupant mental health in isolation, and equitable access to essential life-support systems.
activities.scaffolding: Sustainability Lens Definitions: Ecological (preserving natural resources, biodiversity, and ecosystem health). Economic (achieving financial viability, lifecycle cost efficiency, and long-term asset value). Social (enhancing human wellbeing, social ethics, community equity, and occupant health).
activities.eLearning: Project the Livingstone Shire Council Sustainability Policy statement on the whiteboard to demonstrate real-world application of these lenses in local planning.
activities.transition: Transition from theoretical definitions to the practical application of these lenses by conducting a brief audit of your 'Doomsday Shelter' material choices.

Model the check-listing process for the concrete option using the criteria provided on the board.

activities.questioning:
question: If local concrete has a lower transport footprint than imported timber, does it become the more 'Ecological' choice?
expected: Yes, because the embodied energy saved from reduced logistics often outweighs the energy intensity of production itself.
question: How does the 'Social' lens view the use of treated timber in an extreme environment?
expected: It involves human safety and health; materials must be non-toxic and durable to ensure the wellbeing of the inhabitants.

activities.questioning:
question: How does the thermal mass of your flooring material influence the shelter's internal temperature regulation throughout the day?
expected: High thermal mass materials like concrete absorb heat during the day and release it at night, stabilising internal temperatures, whereas low mass materials fluctuate quickly.
question: In what way does your choice of exterior wall cladding affect the long-term economic viability of the shelter?

activities.scaffolding:
Definitions for Reference:

- Social Sustainability: Ensuring the material provides a safe, healthy, and comfortable environment for users.

activities.title: Creating Annotations
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the precise use of the 'Text' and 'Leader' tools in SketchUp to create clear, professional annotations. activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Select the 'Text' tool in SketchUp. 2. Click the feature to be identified. 3. Input text using the following format: Feature Name | Sustainability Lens (Ecological, Economic, or Social) | Brief justification of sustainability impact.

Expected: Because the shelter's lifespan and energy performance are heavily dependent on raw material properties and their lifecycle impacts.
activities.scaffolding: Sustainability Lens definitions: 1. Ecological: Relates to resource preservation, carbon footprint, and energy efficiency. 2. workbookSpec.modelAnswer: Ensure all four categories are present; if any are missing, the design justification will be deemed incomplete for summative assessment purposes.

lessons.learningGoal: Develop a sequenced time and action plan for the Doomsday Shelter project.

activities.title: Defining Project Terms
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that rigorous project management distinguishes a professional design proposal from a casual concept. Define the core metrics: milestones as checkpoints, the critical path as the backbone of the timeline, and task sequencing as the logical dependency of work. Model an example: 'If we skip the critical path identification, we cannot guarantee the project completion date. For your shelter, a milestone would be submitting your final orthogonal drawings.'
activities.studentsDo: Complete the project management terminology table. Students must provide a concise technical definition and apply it specifically to the Doomsday Shelter project workflow.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Research or recall the definition for each project management term. 2. Record how each specific term applies to the construction of your Doomsday Shelter.
activities.questioning: Why might a 'milestone' be more effective than a simple checklist? Expected: Milestones act as validation points to confirm specific project phases are ready for the next stage. How does the 'critical path' influence your timeline? Expected: It isolates the sequence of tasks that have zero slack; any delay here directly impacts the final delivery date.
activities.scaffolding: Milestone: A specific point in time marking a major achievement or completion of a project phase. Critical Path: The sequence of dependent tasks that defines the minimum amount of time needed to complete the project. Task Sequencing: The logical ordering of project activities based on dependencies.
activities.eLearning: Monitor students accessing the Project Management Plan template.
activities.transition: Transition to drafting your own sequenced time and action plan.

Task Sequencing: The logical flow of work based on dependencies. Shelter Context: Framing must be constructed before external cladding is installed.

activities.title: SketchUp Scenes Modelling
activities.teacherDoes: Explain the necessity of technical documentation standards in engineering. Model the 'Scenes' tool in SketchUp: 1. Navigate to Camera > Parallel Projection. 2. Set view to standard isometric. 3. Open Scenes panel and click '+' to save. Model the difference between Parallel Projection (true scale, orthogonal) and Perspective (foreshortened, spatial visualization). Provide the 'Annotate' worksheet showing a sample orthographic projection of a previous project, demonstrating how to label 'Elevation' vs 'Plan' views.
activities.studentsDo: Observe the demonstration on the projector. Open their SketchUp project file. Configure their first 'Front Elevation' scene using Parallel Projection. Save this scene for their design evidence documentation.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Set Camera to Parallel Projection.
2. Align model to Standard View > Front.
3. Open Scenes tray (Window > Default Tray > Scenes).
4. Click '+' to create a Scene, rename to 'Front Elevation'.
5. Annotate your provided worksheet using the 4 numbered callouts to identify technical elements.
activities.questioning: Why is parallel projection essential for manufacturing? Expected: It preserves true edge lengths, allowing for accurate measurement and scaling. When is a 3D perspective view most effective for a stakeholder? Expected: During the initial concept approval phase to convey spatial 'look and feel' and scale.
activities.scaffolding: Camera Modes: Parallel Projection (No foreshortening, used for technical plans) vs Perspective (Has vanishing points, used for visual renders). Technical Drawing Elements: Plan View (Top down), Elevation (Side view), Isometric (30-degree angle for 3D representation).

workbookSpec.title: Analysing Orthographic Projections
workbookSpec.prompt: Identify and explain the four key features of the provided orthogonal drawing on the worksheet.
workbookSpec.modelAnswer: 1. Projection Line (indicates alignment between views); 2. Dimensioning (identifies length of component); 3. Hidden Detail (shows interior structure); 4. Elevation (shows exterior face).
workbookSpec.figureHint: A multi-view orthographic drawing of a basic bracket or block component.

activities.workbookMaterials: SketchUp Camera Guide & View Analysis Worksheet.
activities.teacherAnswerKey: 1. Elevation View: Represents the front face of the object. 2. Plan View: Shows the object from directly above. 3. Hidden Line: Represented by dashed lines to show internal edges. 4. Dimensioning: Provides exact scale measurements for manufacture.

activities.title: Guided Scene Creation
activities.teacherDoes: Demonstrate the precise method for generating orthogonal and perspective views in SketchUp. Explain: 'Orthogonal views remove perspective distortion, allowing for accurate measurement verification.' Model the workflow: 1. Navigate to Camera > Standard Views > Top. 2. Adjust field of view to 0 (Parallel Projection). 3. Save as Scene. 4. Toggle to Isometric for the 3D presentation view. Verify students are correctly naming their scenes for the final technical report document.
activities.studentsDo: Follow the teacher demonstration to configure SketchUp camera settings, apply Parallel Projection for orthogonal views, and establish specific named scenes for their project documentation.
activities.visibleInstructions: 1. Navigate to Camera menu and set Standard Views to Top. 2. Enable Parallel Projection via Camera menu. 3. Open Scenes panel and create a new scene named 'Plan View'. 4. Rotate model to Isometric view. 5. Create a second scene named 'Isometric View'. 6. Verify all scene names correspond to the checklist requirements.
activities.questioning: Why is Parallel Projection critical for orthogonal drawing? Expected: It eliminates perspective foreshortening, ensuring dimensions represent true scale. How does naming scenes improve workflow efficiency? Expected: It enables instant recall of specific viewports, preventing re-alignment errors during final exports.
activities.scaffolding: Orthogonal Projection: Views representing a 3D object from specific 2D planes (Top, Front, Side). Parallel Projection: A camera setting where parallel lines remain parallel, essential for scale drawings. Perspective View: A view that mimics human eye perception, showing depth and scale variation.

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Ecological Sustainability: Example Answer: Use of permeable paving allows groundwater recharge, meeting the resource efficiency criteria. activities.title: Sustainability Continuum

Model the placement of a generic design (e.g., a plastic water bottle) on the continuum, noting how it might score high on economic efficiency but low on ecological impact due to material choices. Guide students to apply this evaluative thinking to their specific design solutions.
activities.studentsDo: Assess your design solution against the three pillars of sustainability (Ecological, Economic, and Social). Plot your project on the provided continuum and provide a concise justification for the rating.

expected: Lower costs often result from mass-produced, non-biodegradable materials, creating a tension between project affordability and environmental responsibility.
activities.scaffolding: Sustainability Pillars: Ecological (environmental impact, resource efficiency), Economic (viability, cost-effectiveness, longevity), Social (community benefit, accessibility, user well-being). Scale: 1 (Minimal/Needs improvement) to 5 (High/Optimal performance).

activities.title: Defining Communication Conventions
activities.teacherDoes: Explain that technical drawings require strict adherence to standard conventions to ensure interoperability between design teams and stakeholders. How does a legend improve the clarity of an annotated diagram? Expected: It separates complex detail from the main drawing, preventing visual clutter and ensuring professional readability.

question: What happens if an annotated diagram lacks a measurable scale or reference?

activities.scaffolding:
Principles of Technical Communication:
1. Technical Clarity: Unambiguous graphical representation.
2. Scale: Accurate sizing relative to reality.
3. Justification: Evidence-based reasoning for design decisions.
4. Constraints: Adherence to predefined limitations (budget, site, materials).
5. Professional Standard: Industry-appropriate aesthetic and detail.

workbookSpec.title: Design Process Evaluation (3-2-1)
workbookSpec.prompt: Reflect on your Doomsday Shelter project development. Evaluate your design process by identifying key successes and areas for future growth.

sections.label: 3 Strengths of your shelter design:
2 Specific improvements made to your design during the development process (and why):
1 Key lesson learned for future engineering projects:

activities.teacherAnswerKey: Model Answer: 3 Strengths: (1) Integrated rainwater harvesting system reduces reliance on external supply. (2) Use of recycled steel cladding aligns with sustainability criteria. (3) Vaulted roof geometry effectively sheds high-velocity debris. 2 Improvements: (1) Changed foundation depth from 300mm to 500mm after researching soil liquefaction risks. (2) Replaced PVC piping with copper to ensure fire resistance. 1 Key Lesson: Prioritising material research before finalising SketchUp geometry would save time on re-drawing iterations.

activities.title: Final Submission
activities.teacherDoes: Guide students through the 'final submission protocol'. Model the verification process: open the submitted file from the LMS preview window to confirm file integrity and orientation of pages. Emphasize: 'Do not rely on the file name; verify the file content.'
activities.studentsDo: Follow the submission protocol, verify the uploaded PDF, confirm the status change in the LMS, and save a local version to their personal drive or cloud storage.
activities.visibleInstructions:
1. Upload PDF to the LMS.
2. Open your submission via the portal preview to check for missing pages.
3. Confirm status is 'Submitted'.
4. Create a backup copy.
activities.questioning:
Why is verifying the file content post-upload more effective than just checking the file name? Expected: File names can be misleading; verifying the content ensures the correct draft is submitted and no pages are corrupted during upload.
How does maintaining a backup file demonstrate professional accountability? Expected: It safeguards against data loss and serves as a verified record of your work for future audits or feedback discussions.
activities.scaffolding:
Checklist items:
- File format: .pdf
- File size: < 20MB
- Naming convention: [Surname]_[Firstname]_Assessment3.pdf
- Content: Cover page, project rationale, SketchUp models, diagrams, evaluation.
activities.eLearning: Monitor LMS backend for 'Submitted' status updates. Provide immediate feedback if a student uploads an incorrect file type or corrupted file.
